title: Pharmacogenomics: Right Drug, Right Dose
summary: How genetic variation in drug-metabolizing enzymes shapes drug response and prevents adverse events.

content_blocks.text: Why the Same Drug Causes Toxicity in Some and Fails in Others

Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) cause over 100,000 deaths and 2 million hospitalizations annually in the United States. An estimated 7% of ADRs are attributable to pharmacogenomic (PGx) variation — predictable, preventable differences in how individuals metabolize and respond to medications based on genetic variants in drug-metabolizing enzymes, transporters, and targets.

content_blocks.label: Americans carry at least one actionable PGx variant
content_blocks.context: CPIC (Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium) guidelines cover >90 drug-gene pairs; PGx affects virtually every major drug class

content_blocks.text: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes in the liver metabolize approximately 75% of all clinically used drugs. Key CYP genes with well-established clinical PGx include CYP2D6 (antidepressants, antipsychotics, codeine, tamoxifen), CYP2C19 (clopidogrel, PPIs, SSRIs), CYP2C9 (warfarin, NSAIDs), and CYP3A4/5 (statins, immunosuppressants, many oncology drugs).

rows: No functional enzyme — variant alleles on both copies
Drug accumulates → toxicity; prodrugs fail (e.g., codeine → no morphine)
Reduced enzyme activity — one functional + one non-functional allele
Elevated drug exposure; increased ADR risk
Expected drug response at standard doses
Gene duplication — markedly increased enzyme activity
Drug cleared too fast → therapeutic failure; prodrug toxicity risk

content_blocks.text: Codeine and CYP2D6: Codeine is a prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Ultrarapid metabolizers (1–7% of Europeans, up to 29% of North Africans) produce dangerous morphine levels. The FDA black-boxed codeine in nursing mothers and children post-tonsillectomy. Poor metabolizers receive no analgesia. CPIC Guidelines recommend alternative opioids for both extreme phenotypes.

content_blocks.body: Clopidogrel (Plavix) is a prodrug requiring CYP2C19 activation to its active antiplatelet metabolite. CYP2C19 poor and intermediate metabolizers (20–30% of patients) have reduced activation and higher rates of stent thrombosis. The FDA added a black box warning in 2010. CPIC and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend prasugrel or ticagrelor for PCI patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.
content_blocks.title: Clopidogrel and CYP2C19: A High-Stakes Example

content_blocks.text: Warfarin dosing is jointly influenced by CYP2C9 (metabolism), VKORC1 (target sensitivity), and CYP4F2 (vitamin K processing). The FDA-approved warfarin label includes PGx dosing tables. Multiple clinical decision support algorithms (Gage, International Warfarin Pharmacogenomics Consortium) incorporate these variants to predict therapeutic dose, reducing time-to-therapeutic INR.
